cards.front: Recall a key point about Dynamics Texture and Sonority
cards.back: Texture describes how musical lines combine: monophonic (single line), homophonic (melody + chords), polyphonic (independent lines), antiphonal (spatially separated groups).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Dynamics Texture and Sonority
cards.back: Sonority (timbre) is the unique sound quality of each instrument or voice — same notes sound different on violin vs clarinet vs voice.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Dynamics Texture and Sonority
cards.back: Dynamics shape musical expression: crescendo builds intensity; diminuendo releases it; sudden changes (sfz) create drama and surprise.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Dynamics Texture and Sonority
cards.back: Instrumental techniques change sonority: arco (bowed) vs pizzicato (plucked) on strings; con sordino (muted) brass; palm mute on guitar; falsetto voice.

cards.front: What should you know about music exam tips?
cards.back: Name the TEXTURE type (monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic etc). Identify INSTRUMENTAL TECHNIQUES by name (arco, pizzicato, con sordino). Track DYNAMIC changes and their emotional effect.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Texture means how thick or thin the music sounds. Correct: Texture has specific TYPE vocabulary: monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic, imitative, canonic, antiphonal, layered, melody and accompaniment. Always identify the TYPE and explain its effect. Thin or thick describes density, not texture — use the correct terminology.
Analyse the texture and sonority of a piece of music. Identify specific textural types and instrumental/vocal techniques. Explain how they contribute to the music's effect.
